232.title: Up the mountain (Matthew 5:1–2)
232.hook: he sits down, the way a rabbi teaches, and opens his mouth
232.howItsDone: Christians read the Sermon on the Mount often; many churches hear parts of it through the year, and some Christians read all three chapters at once, slowly, as a whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of camp four, back to Galilee, and your line was: start again knowing more. What did you see in something familiar? Now camp five: the depths. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Think about how you can tell a talk is about to matter. The speaker stops pacing. Pulls up a chair. Sits down. Everyone leans in. For the next six weeks we're going somewhere new: the Sermon on the Mount, chapters five, six and seven of Matthew's Gospel. It's the longest block of Jesus's teaching in the Bible, and probably the most quoted. Blessed are the meek. Turn the other cheek. Salt and light. The Lord's Prayer. Treasure where moth and rust corrupt. The house on the rock. Words people use without knowing where they come from. And Matthew sets the scene in just two verses.
screen: `SOMEONE SITS DOWN; EVERYONE LEANS IN.` → `MATTHEW 5 TO 7.` → `WORDS EVERYONE QUOTES.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain: and when he was set, his disciples came unto him: And he opened his mouth, and taught them, saying." Three small details, and each one is doing something. First, he went up into a mountain. Matthew's first readers, many of them Jewish, would think of another teacher who went up a mountain: Moses on Sinai, receiving the law. Matthew seems to want that echo. Here's a new teacher on a mountain, giving teaching about how to live. Matthew never names the mountain. Tradition places it on a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum, and a church stands there today. Second, when he was set: when he sat down. Today a speaker stands to show authority. In his world, a teacher sat. Jesus sits down in the synagogue at Nazareth to teach, and he later speaks of teachers who sit in Moses' seat. Sitting down means: class is in session. Third, he opened his mouth. It sounds redundant; how else would he speak? But it's an old, solemn way of saying, what follows is weighty. It's like saying, and he began. Luke has a shorter version of some of the same teaching, set on a level place, and many readers think both gospels are gathering sayings Jesus taught many times. Either way, the posture is the point. Before the disciples hear a single word, they come close. The first move of the whole sermon isn't doing anything. It's coming near and listening.
screen: `HE WENT UP INTO A MOUNTAIN.` · `WHEN HE WAS SET: HE SAT DOWN.` · `HE OPENED HIS MOUTH.` · `THE DISCIPLES CAME NEAR.` · then, large: `AND HE OPENED HIS MOUTH, AND TAUGHT THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit down to listen. Wherever you are, sit, if you're not already. Let your feet rest on the ground. Put your phone face down. For these two minutes, you're not going to answer anything, fix anything or plan anything. Just listen: to the room, to your breath, to what's underneath the noise. If you pray, you can come near, the way the disciples did, and let God speak first. The bell holds the time.
Up the mountain. Where Jesus sits down, the way a teacher did, to begin the Sermon on the Mount.
Your line: sit down, listen. Today, in one conversation, sit down for it, if you can, and let the other person finish before you say a word. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: The poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3)
233.hook: blessed are the poor in spirit: the empty-handed have room for the kingdom
233.howItsDone: Many Christians know the Beatitudes by heart; Orthodox churches sing them in the Divine Liturgy most Sundays, and they're read in many churches on All Saints' Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus went up the mountain and sat down, and your line was sit down, listen. Did you let someone finish before you spoke? Day two hundred thirty-three.

Hashtag blessed. You've seen it under photos of a new car, a beach, a baby, a promotion. Blessed means things are going well. So imagine sitting on that hillside. The crowd is full of fishermen, farmers, the sick and the poor. Jesus has just sat down, and everyone leans in for the first words of his great sermon. And he opens with a list of people who are blessed. Only the list doesn't include anyone with a new car. It starts with the people who have nothing.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `THE FIRST WORDS OF THE SERMON.` → `IT STARTS WITH THE EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." This is the first of the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, blessed. Matthew's Greek word is makarios. It meant happy, fortunate, well off, the word Greeks used for the gods and the rich. And its Hebrew cousin opens the book of Psalms: blessed is the man. So when Jesus says makarios, it's partly a congratulation. Lucky you. You're in a good place. Then look who he congratulates. The Greek word for poor here doesn't mean a little short this month. It's the word for a beggar, someone with empty hands. Luke's version just says blessed be ye poor. Matthew adds in spirit, and Christians have read that in more than one way. Some hear the humble: people who know they can't earn their way to God. Others hear those who are poor and have no pride left to hold on to. Many read both together. Either way, it's the opposite of self-sufficient. And the promise isn't someday. It's theirs is the kingdom of heaven, present tense. Here's the picture that helps. You can't receive a gift with your hands full. If you're clutching your phone, your coffee and your bags, someone has to wait while you put something down. The poor in spirit already have their hands open. That's why this beatitude comes first. Everything else in the sermon is a gift, and it's the empty hands that can take it.
screen: `MAKARIOS: BLESSED, FORTUNATE.` · `POOR: A BEGGAR'S EMPTY HANDS.` · `IN SPIRIT: TWO READINGS.` · `THEIRS IS THE KINGDOM, NOW.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one need. Settle, and breathe. Rest your hands on your knees, palms open, facing up. Now think of one thing you can't do on your own right now. Help you need, and haven't asked for. Something you can't fix. Just name it, quietly, to yourself. No shame in it. Let your open hands say what's true: I don't have everything. If you pray, you can bring that need to God with your hands open. The bell holds the time.
Blessed. Makarios in Greek: fortunate, well off, congratulations. And Jesus says it first to the poor in spirit.
Your line: empty hands can receive. Today, ask one person for help with something real, and let yourself receive it without paying it back right away. Day two hundred thirty-three.

234.title: Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4)
234.hook: blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted
234.howItsDone: Christians keep funerals and memorial prayers for the dead, and many churches hold services for those grieving, especially around All Souls' Day or in the dark weeks before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word of the sermon, blessed, and your line was empty hands can receive. Did you let someone help you? Day two hundred thirty-four.

Most of us have learned how to grieve politely. A few days off work. A card. Then, gently, the world expects you to be fine. People say, stay strong, or at least they're in a better place, and mean it kindly. But sometimes what you need is for someone to let you be sad. The second line of Jesus's sermon goes somewhere most of us would never think to go. After the empty-handed, he congratulates the people who are crying.
screen: `GRIEVING POLITELY.` → `STAY STRONG.` → `THE SECOND LINE OF THE SERMON.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The Greek word for mourn is the strongest word the language had for grief. It's what you do at a funeral, out loud, not a quiet sigh. And Jesus doesn't say, blessed are those who get over it. He says, blessed are those who mourn. Christians have read this in a few ways. It's grief for someone you've lost. It's also grief over the wrong in the world, and over your own wrongs; many early Christian teachers read it that way. And the prophet Isaiah had promised one who would come to comfort all that mourn. Jesus seems to be saying: that's now. Here's the second word worth opening. Comforted in Greek comes from parakaleo: to call to your side. It's the same family as the word John's Gospel uses for the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, which the King James Bible translates the Comforter. So comfort here isn't a pat on the back from across the room. It's someone called in to sit beside you. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say you won't mourn. It doesn't say your grief is wrong or weak. Jesus himself wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus. Paul later tells Christians not to sorrow as others which have no hope: not to stop sorrowing, but to sorrow with hope. That's the beatitude: grief that is real, and grief that isn't the last word. Mourning is not the end.
screen: `MOURN: THE LOUDEST GRIEF.` · `FOR THE LOST, AND FOR THE WRONG.` · `COMFORT: CALLED TO YOUR SIDE.` · `GRIEF WITH HOPE.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone grieving. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who has lost something this year: a person, a marriage, a job, their health. Picture them. Don't plan a speech. Just ask yourself: what would it look like to sit beside them? A message that says, I'm thinking of you, no reply needed. A meal. A walk. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Those who mourn. The second beatitude: the ones who grieve out loud are blessed, because someone will come to their side.
Your line: mourning is not the end. Today, reach out to one grieving person, and don't try to fix it. Just come to their side. Day two hundred thirty-four.

235.title: The meek (Matthew 5:5)
235.hook: meek means strength held gently, not weakness
235.howItsDone: Christians often name meekness, or gentleness, among the virtues they pray for; Paul lists it as a fruit of the Spirit, and many Christians practice it as holding back anger and not insisting on their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, those who mourn, and your line was mourning is not the end. Did you come to someone's side? Day two hundred thirty-five.

Nobody puts meek on a resume. It sounds like the kid who gets his lunch money taken. Mousy, timid, a pushover. Meek and mild. In most offices, the meek do not inherit anything; they get talked over in meetings. So the third line of the sermon lands strangely. Jesus says the meek are blessed, and not only that: they're going to inherit the whole earth. Either the world has meek wrong, or the sermon does. Let's look at the word.
screen: `NOBODY PUTS MEEK ON A RESUME.` → `MEEK AND MILD.` → `THEY'LL INHERIT THE EARTH?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." First, this isn't new. It's almost word for word from Psalm 37: "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace." In that psalm, the meek are people who don't fret about the wicked getting ahead, and don't grab for themselves; they wait for God. Now the Greek word, praus. Greek writers used it for a gentle person, and for a wild animal tamed, a horse that has learned to take the bridle. A tamed horse isn't weak. It's every bit as strong as before. The difference is that its strength is under control, not thrashing around. That's meek: strength, held gently. Look at who the Bible calls meek. Moses, of all people: the book of Numbers says he was very meek, above all the men on the face of the earth. The man who stood up to Pharaoh. And Jesus says of himself, I am meek and lowly in heart. The same Jesus who turned over tables in the temple. So meek can't mean spineless. It means someone who could hit back and doesn't; who could take and doesn't; who doesn't need to win every argument to know who they are. And the promise? They shall inherit the earth. Inherit is a gift word. You don't seize an inheritance; it's given to you. The grabbers take and take. The meek receive.
screen: `FROM PSALM 37.` · `PRAUS: A HORSE THAT TAKES THE BRIDLE.` · `MOSES, VERY MEEK.` · `INHERIT: GIVEN, NOT SEIZED.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL INHERIT THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold back one sharp word. Settle, and breathe. Think of the person who most easily gets under your skin. Picture a moment today where they might say the thing that sets you off. Notice the sharp reply that's already loaded. Feel its strength. You could say it. Now, picture holding it, the way a rider holds the reins. Not swallowing it forever. Just not letting it bolt. If you pray, you can ask for gentleness. The bell holds the time.
Meek. Praus in Greek: not weak, but gentle strength, like a strong horse that takes the bridle.
Your line: strength, held gently. Today, the next time a sharp word is ready to fly, hold the reins for one breath, and choose a gentler one. Day two hundred thirty-five.
